idiom_name: protocol factory with concrete family types (Cocoa class clusters are the library cousin)
implementation_notes: A protocol declares one creation requirement per product kind and each family is a struct or class conforming to it; the chosen family is injected or held as `any UIFactory` for runtime selection, or as a generic parameter/`some` for static dispatch. Foundation's class clusters (NSNumber, NSString, NSArray) are the library realization of the same idea - one public abstract superclass dispensing private concrete subclasses - but pure Swift cannot recreate them, because initializers cannot return a sibling type (the swift-evolution thread closed that door). Use `any` at API boundaries and generics internally to avoid existential boxing. For factory initializers that return `Self`, use the `init` call pattern rather than a separate static factory method when the initializer can validate and throw for invalid arguments.
pitfalls: `any` existentials can add dynamic dispatch or storage overhead; class references are already references, while protocols with associated types need type erasure or generics, so choose the boundary deliberately.

Foundation class clusters must be subclassed by overriding primitive methods only, and the cluster's initializer decides the concrete subclass; substituting a family means replacing the whole cluster, not one product.
Returning class products from protocols brings ARC, reference identity and inheritability into tests; struct-based product families are often easier to fake.

An API returning `some UIFactory` commits all calls to one hidden concrete family and cannot select families at runtime; use `any UIFactory` at the runtime boundary and opaque/generic types internally when static dispatch is wanted.
